items.stem: Which term describes Durkheim’s term for the shared beliefs, values and norms that bind a society together?
items.answer: Collective conscience
items.markingKey: Collective conscience: Durkheim’s term for the shared beliefs, values and norms that bind a society together. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “functional alternative”, and give one example.
items.answer: Something that performs the same functions as religion. Example: nationalism or sport creating solidarity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (something that performs the same functions as religion); 1 mark for a relevant example such as nationalism or sport creating solidarity. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “life crises” and “social solidarity”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Life crises: events such as death that create stress, which religion helps people cope with (Malinowski) (e.g. funeral rituals comforting mourners). Social solidarity: the sense of belonging and integration that binds members of society together (e.g. a nation mourning together after a disaster).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: After a terrorist attack in Santiago, people of many faiths and none gather in the main square, light candles, hold a minute’s silence and sing the national anthem. Suggest how a functionalist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Functionalism: religion promotes social solidarity and value consensus, helps people cope with life crises and reinforces the collective conscience (Durkheim, Malinowski, Parsons).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Fishermen in a village near Manila hold a religious ceremony before every long voyage out to sea, but not before fishing in the calm harbour. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: religion promotes social solidarity and value consensus, helps people cope with life crises and reinforces the collective conscience (Durkheim, Malinowski, Parsons).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Fishermen in a village near Santiago hold a religious ceremony before every long voyage out to sea, but not before fishing in the calm harbour. Compare how postmodernist and Marxist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: religion has become a matter of individual choice and consumption; people pick and mix beliefs in a spiritual supermarket (Lyon, Heelas). Marxism: religion is ideology that legitimates class inequality and offers false comfort to the oppressed (“the opium of the people”), creating false consciousness (Marx, Lenin).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of structured interviews for studying participation in national ceremonies.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; every respondent is asked the same questions in the same order, so results are standardised and reliable. Limitations: the interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers; the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying participation in national ceremonies but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using covert participant observation to research the role of religious festivals in community life.
items.answer: Strengths: it produces rich, first-hand qualitative data with high validity; because the group does not know it is being studied, members act naturally and the Hawthorne effect is avoided. Limitations: note-taking is difficult, so data depends on memory and may be inaccurate; the study cannot be repeated, so reliability is low. Theory: covert participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the role of religious festivals in community life but best combined with another method such as content analysis (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Define the term “opium of the people”, and give one example.
items.answer: Marx’s description of religion as a comfort that dulls the pain of exploitation without curing it. Example: promises of rewards in heaven for the poor.

items.stem: Distinguish between “ideology” and “opium of the people”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Ideology: a set of ideas that justifies the interests of a powerful group (e.g. the belief that social positions are ordained by God). Opium of the people: Marx’s description of religion as a comfort that dulls the pain of exploitation without curing it (e.g. promises of rewards in heaven for the poor).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A preacher in Istanbul tells poor factory workers that their suffering will be rewarded in heaven and that they should obey their employers. Suggest how a Weberian sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Weberian theory: religious ideas can either legitimate the existing order or motivate change; the poor may be drawn to a theodicy of disprivilege, but religious ideas and leaders can also inspire social movements.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A preacher in Kathmandu tells poor factory workers that their suffering will be rewarded in heaven and that they should obey their employers. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: religion integrates society around shared values; whether teaching acceptance or community action, it binds believers together and helps them cope with hardship.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Priests in villages near Cairo help landless farmers organise against wealthy landowners, quoting scripture to argue that God sides with the poor. Compare how Weberian and neo-Marxist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Weberian theory: religious ideas can either legitimate the existing order or motivate change; the poor may be drawn to a theodicy of disprivilege, but religious ideas and leaders can also inspire social movements. Neo-Marxism: religion is relatively autonomous: it can support ruling-class hegemony, but clergy may side with the oppressed and religion can inspire resistance, as in liberation theology (Maduro, Gramsci).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using semi-structured interviews to research the political views of religious leaders.
items.answer: Strengths: open follow-up questions let interviewees explain their reasoning; the interviewer can probe and clarify answers, which improves validity. Limitations: interviewer bias may still affect answers; follow-up questions differ between interviews, so reliability is lower than with a fixed schedule. Theory: semi-structured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative and quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the political views of religious leaders but best combined with another method such as content analysis (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: A research team is investigating the political views of religious leaders. Evaluate the use of self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; closed, pre-coded questions produce quantitative data that is easy to compare and turn into statistics. Limitations: pre-set answers cannot capture the subjective meanings people attach to their experiences; response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the political views of religious leaders but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using unstructured interviews to research the link between religious values and business success.
items.answer: Strengths: they allow people to explain the meanings they give to their experiences in their own words; the interviewer can follow up answers and explore meanings in the interviewee’s own words. Limitations: they cannot measure patterns across a large population because only a few people can be interviewed; the interviewer may lead the interviewee or interpret answers selectively (interviewer bias). Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the link between religious values and business success but best combined with another method such as official statistics (triangulation).

items.stem: Lina, a sociology student, is designing a project on the link between religious values and business success. Evaluate the use of official statistics for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they give national data on whole populations that no single researcher could collect; they are usually free and readily available, saving time and money. Limitations: they cannot tell us how people feel or why they act as they do; they show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the link between religious values and business success but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).

items.stem: A survey of 300 religious adults in Accra asked about religion and inequality. Table: religious adults agreeing (%) | Lowest income group | Highest income group. Agree that inequality is “God’s will” | 30% | 20%. Agree that the poor will be rewarded after death | 52% | 36%. Support protests against poverty | 43% | 33%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Lowest income group and Highest income group for Support protests against poverty. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that religion acts as an ideology that discourages the poor from challenging inequality.
items.answer: (a) 33 − 43 = -10 percentage points (Highest income group compared with Lowest income group). (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is lower for Highest income group than for Lowest income group among Agree that inequality is “God’s will”, Agree that the poor will be rewarded after death, Support protests against poverty; Agree that the poor will be rewarded after death had the highest figure for Highest income group. Beliefs about rewards after death may reduce pressure for change. Qualifications: Many poor believers support protests; survey cannot show cause; attitudes vary between religions; social desirability. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 300 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.

items.stem: A survey of 450 adults in Karachi compared regular attenders with those who never attend religious services. Table: adults agreeing (%) | Attend services regularly | Never attend. Feel they belong to their community | 68% | 49%. Have helped a neighbour in the last month | 60% | 45%. Trust most people | 50% | 40%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Attend services regularly and Never attend for Feel they belong to their community. (b) Explain one limitation of using self-completion questionnaires to collect data like these. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that religion promotes social solidarity.
items.answer: (a) 49 − 68 = -19 percentage points (Never attend compared with Attend services regularly). (b) Response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure is lower for Never attend than for Attend services regularly among Feel they belong to their community, Have helped a neighbour in the last month, Trust most people; Feel they belong to their community had the highest figure for Never attend. Shared worship builds social solidarity (Durkheim). Qualifications: Correlation is not causation: sociable people may be more likely to attend; religion may unite insiders but exclude outsiders; self-report. The data also come from self-completion questionnaires of 450 adults in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 68 and 49; 1 mark for 19 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes a distorted view of reality that prevents the oppressed from seeing their exploitation?
items.answer: False consciousness
items.markingKey: False consciousness: a distorted view of reality that prevents the oppressed from seeing their exploitation. [1]

items.stem: Outline what Lenin meant by arguing that religion is “spiritual gin” used by the ruling class to keep the working class in its place.
items.answer: Lenin argued the ruling class uses religion to manipulate the masses.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the idea; 1 mark for developing it: Lenin argued the ruling class uses religion to manipulate the masses. [2]

items.stem: Priests in villages near Jakarta help landless farmers organise against wealthy landowners, quoting scripture to argue that God sides with the poor. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Marxism: religion usually acts as ideology: it legitimates class inequality and offers false comfort (“the opium of the people”); where religion is used by the poor against the rich, it shows that religion reflects the class struggle of its society, and Marx saw it as “the sigh of the oppressed creature” (Marx, Lenin).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Chloe surveyed 500 people who attend religious services in Toronto. Table: religious adults agreeing (%) | Lowest income group | Highest income group. Agree that inequality is “God’s will” | 34% | 29%. Agree that the poor will be rewarded after death | 53% | 37%. Support protests against poverty | 42% | 22%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Lowest income group and Highest income group for Agree that the poor will be rewarded after death (Highest income group minus Lowest income group)?
items.answer: -16 percentage points
items.markingKey: 37 − 53 = -16 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of participant observation for studying the political views of religious leaders.
items.answer: Strengths: it reveals the meanings and labels that shape interaction as it happens; it is often the only way to study small or closed groups in depth. Limitations: it cannot measure the extent of a pattern across a whole society; it is time-consuming, costly and may put the researcher at risk. Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the political views of religious leaders but best combined with another method such as longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the rational pursuit of profit for its own sake, which Weber linked to the Protestant ethic?
items.answer: Spirit of capitalism
items.markingKey: Spirit of capitalism: the rational pursuit of profit for its own sake, which Weber linked to the Protestant ethic. [1]

items.stem: Explain Weber’s argument about the Protestant ethic and the spirit of capitalism.
items.answer: Calvinists believed in predestination, causing salvation anxiety; they worked hard, lived ascetically and reinvested profits as a sign of God’s favour, creating the rational spirit of capitalism.
items.markingKey: 1 mark predestination; 1 mark anxiety; 1 mark ascetic hard work; 1 mark link to capitalism. [4]

items.stem: Religious leaders in Hanoi lead peaceful marches against laws that discriminate against an ethnic minority, using sermons to mobilise support. Suggest how a Weberian sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Weberian theory: religious ideas can bring about social change; beliefs such as the Protestant ethic shaped economic behaviour, and religion can motivate social movements (Weber).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Members of a strict religious community near Dhaka work long hours, avoid luxury and reinvest their profits; within two generations they own many of the region’s businesses. Explain how a Weberian sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Weberian theory: religious ideas can bring about social change; beliefs such as the Protestant ethic shaped economic behaviour, and religion can motivate social movements (Weber).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of unstructured interviews for studying the link between religious values and business success.
items.answer: Strengths: they allow people to explain the meanings they give to their experiences in their own words; the interviewer can follow up answers and explore meanings in the interviewee’s own words. Limitations: they cannot measure patterns across a large population because only a few people can be interviewed; the interviewer may lead the interviewee or interpret answers selectively (interviewer bias). Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the link between religious values and business success but best combined with another method such as structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: State one example of patriarchy in religion.
items.answer: Restrictions on women’s dress.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. restrictions on women’s dress. [1]

items.stem: Explain two ways in which religion may be patriarchal.
items.answer: Male-dominated leadership and exclusion of women from priesthood; sacred texts written and interpreted by men; rules on women’s dress and sexuality; segregation in places of worship; teachings on women’s domestic roles.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained way. [4]

items.stem: Isla, a university student in Nairobi, chooses to wear the hijab, saying it gives her confidence and protects her from being judged on her looks. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: religion has become a matter of individual choice and consumption; people pick and mix beliefs in a spiritual supermarket (Lyon, Heelas).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A sociologist in Colombo wants to research women’s experiences in religious organisations. Evaluate the use of participant observation for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: it can give access to groups that would never complete a questionnaire, such as deviant subcultures; it is often the only way to study small or closed groups in depth. Limitations: it is time-consuming, costly and may put the researcher at risk; the observer’s presence may change the group’s behaviour (the Hawthorne effect), especially if overt. Theory: participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying women’s experiences in religious organisations but best combined with another method such as official statistics (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]
